PHOTO: ST FILE Published Jun 10, 2026, 03:27 PM Updated Jun 11, 2026, 01:52 PM Set as preferred source Listen SINGAPORE – Sea’s Shopee is cutting hundreds of developer jobs globally, joining rivals across the world in slashing staff while they adopt AI in the workplace and develop new services based on the technology. The reductions, which started this week, amount to about 8 per cent of Shopee’s developer workforce, according to people familiar with the matter. They affect roles such as quality assurance, and more cuts might follow, the people added, asking not to be identified discussing private information. It is unclear if the move is directly tied to Sea’s forays into artificial intelligence. But these coincide with a growing debate about the impact of the technology on jobs across the world, as well as discussions around potential “AI-washing” in the wake of major layoffs at technology companies such as Jack Dorsey’s Block, as well as Oracle. Many tech companies hired aggressively during the pandemic, when online and digital activity boomed and firms struggled to keep pace. At the same time, concerns are growing that AI will reduce a reliance on traditional software tools, eroding the lucrative business of enterprise IT services. While AI usage has not yet translated into clear productivity gains, many companies are seeking ways to do more with less. Sea, the Singapore-headquartered operator of online retailer Shopee and the Garena gaming platform, is making structural shifts after chief executive Forrest Li declared that a trillion-dollar market capitalisation was possible if his company doubled down on AI. It joins a growing number of companies, like rival Alibaba Group, that are investing in AI to catalyse growth while competition in their core business intensifies. A Sea spokesperson said the company regularly reviews and adjusts its staffing needs. “These decisions are always made after careful consideration. For colleagues affected by any changes, we are committed to providing support during this period of transition.” The Creative Media and Publishing Union (CMPU) in Singapore said it was informed in advance about the company’s plans to implement “a workforce adjustment affecting certain employees”. Its spokesperson said that representatives were at Shopee’s office in Geneo on June 8 as well as Sea’s headquarters at One North on June 9 to provide support and assistance to affected union members and employees. “The union is working with the management to ensure that affected members and workers are offered fair compensation packages, and that the adjustment is conducted fairly and responsibly, in accordance with the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower and Responsible Retrenchment.” The Taskforce for Responsible Retrenchment and Employment Facilitation noted that Sea notified the union in advance, and is working closely with CMPU to support affected employees, whose last working day falls between end-June and end-August. “Sea has also committed to providing a retrenchment package in line with the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower and Responsible Retrenchment guidelines.” The company’s stock has taken a beating since September, when it was valued at roughly US$116 billion (S$149 billion), after the recent surge in oil prices dampened consumer sentiment and inflated the cost of operations. Investors are scrutinising its growth trajectory. So far, Sea has been embedding AI in small ways, like through product recommendations and seller tools. In February, the company said it would work with Alphabet’s Google to integrate AI across its operations, including developing AI shopping agents. Sea has also set up dedicated teams to scout for new investments in the technology, people familiar with the matter said in May, as it hunts for its next growth engine beyond e-commerce.
